summary: Specifies new cipher suites, signature algorithms, supported groups and certificate types for TLS 1.2 to support the Russian GOST cryptographic standards. It is a profile for implementers who want interoperable GOST support. The document states it does not imply IETF endorsement of these algorithms. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This lets secure web connections use the cryptography tools from Russian standards, written so implementers can match.

subtitle: Support for Russian cryptographic standards in secure web connections

tldr.problem: Systems requiring Russian cryptographic standards (GOST algorithms) have lacked a standardized specification for using them in TLS 1.2, hindering interoperable implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three cipher suites, two signature algorithms, seven supported elliptic curve groups, and two certificate types that integrate GOST cryptographic algorithms into TLS 1.2 profile, with detailed specifications for record protection, key exchange, and handshake processing.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can now produce interoperable GOST-based TLS 1.2 implementations. The RFC does not imply IETF endorsement of GOST algorithms and applies to jurisdictions requiring their use.

today: RFC 9189 is an informational RFC that remains the current specification for GOST TLS 1.2 cipher suites. It enables interoperable implementations in jurisdictions where Russian cryptographic standards are required. A separate specification for GOST TLS 1.3 is being developed in parallel.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how to use the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms, collectively called GOST, with TLS 1.2 (Transport Layer Security, the protocol that secures web connections). The document defines three cipher suites that combine encryption, authentication, and key exchange algorithms; two signature algorithms based on GOST R 34.10-2012; seven new elliptic curves for key exchange; and two new certificate types for client authentication.

The cipher suites fall into two categories: CTR_OMAC cipher suites use the modern GOST R 34.12-2015 block ciphers (Kuznyechik and Magma), while the CNT_IMIT cipher suite uses the older GOST 28147-89 block cipher. All cipher suites use the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash algorithm. This specification provides a profile of TLS 1.2 enabling implementers in jurisdictions requiring GOST support to produce interoperable implementations. The RFC explicitly states it does not imply IETF endorsement of these algorithms.
sections.eli5: Russian cryptography (GOST) can now work with the TLS standard that protects websites. This tells implementers exactly how to combine the pieces so they all talk to each other.

sections.title: Cipher Suite Definitions and Record Protection
sections.content:
The RFC defines three cipher suites with the following names and hexadecimal values: TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_CTR_OMAC (0xC1, 0x00), TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_MAGMA_CTR_OMAC (0xC1, 0x01), and TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_28147_CNT_IMIT (0xC1, 0x02). Compression is not allowed in any of these cipher suites.

Record protection differs between the two families. The CTR_OMAC cipher suites use a sophisticated key rekeying mechanism called TLSTREE, which derives different encryption and MAC keys for each message using a tree-based key derivation. The CNT_IMIT cipher suite uses the older GOST 28147-89 cipher with a different key derivation approach. Both families use the authenticate-then-encrypt method, which is secure for stream ciphers and must not use the encrypt_then_mac extension.
sections.eli5: The three cipher suites each pick different encryption locks. Each message uses a slightly different key generated from a master key, so breaking one message does not break others.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Handshake
sections.content:
The GOST TLS 1.2 cipher suites use elliptic-curve-based key exchange to establish a shared preliminary secret. The handshake follows the TLS 1.2 protocol flow: the client sends a ClientHello message, the server responds with ServerHello and Server Certificate, and they exchange keys via a ClientKeyExchange message. The server is always authenticated through its certificate; the client is optionally authenticated through the CertificateVerify message.

A critical difference from standard TLS is that the server never sends a ServerKeyExchange message; instead, the server's certificate contains all necessary information for the client to perform the key exchange. The client generates an ephemeral key pair and uses the server's public key to encrypt a preliminary secret. Computations use special key export and key import algorithms (KExp15, KImp15, KExp28147, KImp28147) that wrap the secret in an encrypted and authenticated form. The RFC specifies detailed algorithms for key generation, key exchange generation (KEG and KEG_28147), and MAC computation (gostIMIT28147).
sections.eli5: The client and server shake hands to agree on a secret number. The client encrypts the secret using the server's public key, and the server decrypts it. They use special wrapping methods to protect the secret during exchange.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithms and Parameters
sections.content:
The Kuznyechik cipher suites use the Kuznyechik block cipher with a 16-byte block and 32-byte (256-bit) key. The Magma cipher suites use the Magma cipher with an 8-byte block and 32-byte key. The CNT_IMIT suite uses GOST 28147-89 with an 8-byte block and 32-byte key. All cipher suites use GOST R 34.11-2012 as the hash algorithm with a 256-bit output and PRF_TLS_GOSTR3411_2012_256 as the pseudorandom function.

For encryption, Kuznyechik and Magma suites employ CTR-ACPKM mode (counter mode with algorithm-specific key meshing), while the GOST 28147-89 suite uses CNT (counter) mode with CryptoPro key meshing. Both modes act as stream ciphers. For authentication, the CTR_OMAC suites use OMAC (One-Key MAC, equivalent to CMAC), while the CNT_IMIT suite uses a CBC-MAC-like construction with the gostIMIT28147 algorithm.
sections.eli5: These cipher suites pick specific Russian encryption locks (Kuznyechik, Magma, or GOST 28147-89) and combine them with Russian hashing and authentication algorithms to protect data stream by stream.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms, Curves, and Certificate Types
sections.content:
The RFC introduces two new signature algorithms: gostr34102012_256 (value 64) for GOST R 34.10-2012 with 256-bit keys and gostr34102012_512 (value 65) for 512-bit keys. These are intrinsic signature algorithms, meaning the hash algorithm is built into the signature algorithm. To advertise support, the TLS signature_algorithms extension uses the pairs (8, 64) and (8, 65), where 8 is the special "Intrinsic" hash algorithm value.

The RFC defines seven new elliptic curves for key exchange: GC256A, GC256B, GC256C, GC256D (all 256-bit curves) and GC512A, GC512B, GC512C (512-bit curves), mapped to GOST curve identifiers from RFCs 7836 and 4357. For client authentication, it adds two new certificate types: gost_sign256 (67) for 256-bit GOST signature keys and gost_sign512 (68) for 512-bit keys.
sections.eli5: These suites recognize two Russian signature locks: one with 256-bit keys and one with 512-bit keys. They also define seven elliptic curve groups for key swapping and two ways a client can prove who it is.

sections.title: Additional Algorithms and Historical Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC specifies several supporting algorithms not confined to TLS. The TLSTREE function derives different keys for different messages using nested key derivation functions based on KDF_GOSTR3411_2012_256. The KExp15 and KImp15 algorithms export and import secrets by wrapping them with OMAC authentication and CTR encryption. The KExp28147 and KImp28147 algorithms similarly protect secrets but for the older GOST 28147-89 cipher.

For historical compatibility, the RFC documents that older implementations used different private-use cipher suite values, signature algorithm values, and curve identifiers. The new standardized values (0xC1,0x00 through 0xC1,0x02) allow interoperability going forward. The RFC also lists seven historical curve identifiers that corresponded to GC256B, GC256C, and GC256D under different naming schemes.
sections.eli5: The document includes many helper functions for key wrapping and explains what old implementations used before this standard existed, so people know why the numbers are what they are.
